stem: Based on the text, Okonjo would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus: Forecasters have long estimated the largest hailstones a thunderstorm can produce from the peak speed of its updraft, reasoning that faster-rising air can hold heavier ice aloft. Atmospheric scientist Liesel Okonjo argues that this measure leaves out a key factor. In her simulations, storms with broad updrafts produced larger hail than storms with narrower but faster ones, because a wide updraft keeps a growing stone suspended among supercooled droplets for longer. Speed matters, Okonjo concedes, but only together with the time a stone spends in the zone where it grows.
choices: A storm's peak updraft speed is enough on its own to predict the largest hailstones it can produce.
Two storms with equal peak updraft speeds may still produce hailstones of different maximum sizes.
The speed of a storm's updraft has no effect on the size of the hailstones that the storm produces.
Narrow updrafts keep growing hailstones suspended for longer periods than broad updrafts are able to.
explanation: Okonjo argues that hail size depends on how long a stone stays in the growth zone, which depends on updraft width, not just speed. Extend that to a new case: if two storms have the same speed but different widths, her reasoning predicts different maximum hail sizes. That is what B says.

A.why: This is the forecasters' view that Okonjo is arguing against. You picked the view the passage explains most clearly instead of isolating Okonjo's own claim that speed alone leaves out a key factor.

C.why: You pushed Okonjo's position too far. She concedes that speed matters; her claim is that it isn't the only factor, not that it plays no role.

D.why: This reverses the passage. Okonjo says that wide updrafts keep stones suspended longer, which is why broad updrafts produced larger hail in her simulations.

stem: Based on the text, Arrieta would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus: Planners often judge a new bus lane by how much it shortens the average trip. Urban researcher Tomás Arrieta contends that riders care less about average speed than about predictability. Studying twelve city corridors, he found that ridership rose most where new lanes narrowed the gap between the fastest and slowest trips, even when the average trip barely changed. A route that reliably takes twenty minutes, Arrieta argues, may attract more riders than one that averages fifteen but sometimes takes thirty.
choices: A bus lane is most likely to attract riders when it produces the largest cut in average trip time.
Average trip time has no influence on whether riders decide to use a particular bus route at all.
Ridership grew most on corridors where trip times became more variable after lanes were added.
A bus lane that narrows the range of trip times without shortening the average could raise ridership.
explanation: Arrieta's claim is that predictability drives ridership more than average speed, and his corridors showed ridership rising even when average times barely changed. Apply that to a lane that narrows the range but leaves the average alone, and his reasoning predicts more riders. That is D.

A.why: This is the planners' usual standard, the one Arrieta argues against. You chose the conventional view because the first sentence states it plainly, instead of isolating Arrieta's own claim.

B.why: Arrieta says riders care less about average speed, not that it doesn't matter at all. You turned a claim about which factor matters more into a claim that one factor doesn't count.

C.why: This reverses his finding. Ridership rose most where the spread between fast and slow trips got smaller, not larger.

stem: Based on the text, Sandoval would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus: Astronomers commonly separate giant planets from brown dwarfs by mass: objects above about 13 Jupiter masses, heavy enough to fuse deuterium, are classed as brown dwarfs. Astrophysicist Mira Sandoval argues that this cutoff hides how such objects form. Planets build up within disks of material around young stars, while brown dwarfs collapse directly from gas clouds, as stars do. Sandoval notes that both processes appear able to produce objects on either side of the 13-Jupiter-mass line, and she suggests that classifying by origin would better reflect what these objects are.
choices: An object of 15 Jupiter masses that formed within a disk around a young star could reasonably be called a planet.
Any object that is massive enough to fuse deuterium should be classified as a brown dwarf instead of a planet.
Giant planets and brown dwarfs cannot be meaningfully told apart from each other by any available criterion.
Objects that form within disks around young stars always end up with less than 13 Jupiter masses of material.
explanation: Sandoval wants to classify these objects by how they formed, and planets are the ones that build up in disks. An object that formed in a disk would therefore count as a planet under her scheme, even if its mass puts it above the 13-Jupiter-mass line. That is A, which applies her argument to a new case.

B.why: This is the mass-based cutoff that Sandoval rejects. You picked the conventional criterion because the passage explains it first and clearly.

C.why: Sandoval doesn't say the two can't be told apart. She proposes a better criterion, origin, to replace mass. You pushed 'the current test is flawed' all the way to 'no test works.'

D.why: Sandoval says both formation processes can produce objects on either side of the line, so disk-formed objects can exceed 13 Jupiter masses.

stem: Based on the text, Varga would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus: Paleobotanists often estimate ancient temperatures from fossil leaves, since in living forests the share of species with toothed leaf edges rises as climates get cooler. Paleobotanist Anneke Varga accepts this pattern but argues that temperature is not its only driver. Her survey of modern floras found that plants along rivers and lakeshores bore toothed leaves more often than nearby species on drier ground at the same temperature. Varga suggests that fossil sites formed in wet settings, which are common in the record, may therefore have been read as colder than they actually were.
choices: The share of toothed leaves in a fossil flora is by itself a dependable measure of past temperatures.
The proportion of toothed leaves in a flora is unrelated to the climate in which its plants once grew.
A temperature estimate from leaves preserved in an ancient lakebed may be lower than the true value.
Plants growing on dry ground tend to have toothed leaves more often than plants growing near water.
explanation: Varga argues that wet settings raise the share of toothed leaves, and more toothed leaves get read as a cooler climate. A lakebed is a wet setting, so by her reasoning an estimate from it could come out colder than the real temperature. That is C.

A.why: This is the standard method that Varga argues is incomplete. You chose the view the passage sets up rather than her correction to it.

B.why: Varga accepts the link between toothed leaves and cooler climates and only says temperature is not the only driver. You pushed 'one of several factors' to 'no connection at all.'

D.why: This reverses her survey result. Plants near rivers and lakes had toothed leaves more often than those on drier ground.

stem: Based on the text, Asante-Lund would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus: Linguists often treat two speech varieties as dialects of one language if their speakers can understand each other, and as separate languages if they cannot. Linguist Kwame Asante-Lund argues that this test wrongly assumes understanding runs equally in both directions. In his fieldwork, speakers of one variety understood a neighboring variety far better than its speakers understood them, largely because the first group heard the other's speech regularly on radio and in markets. Intelligibility, he concludes, reflects listeners' exposure as well as how similar two varieties are.
choices: Whether speakers understand each other reliably shows whether their varieties are separate languages.
Mutual intelligibility reveals nothing at all about how similar two speech varieties actually are.
Speakers of two neighboring varieties generally understand each other about equally well.
More contact between two communities could raise intelligibility with no change to their speech.
explanation: Asante-Lund concludes that intelligibility depends partly on exposure, not only on how similar the varieties are. Extend that: if two communities heard each other more, understanding could improve even though neither way of speaking changed. That is D.

A.why: This is the conventional intelligibility test that Asante-Lund challenges. You chose it because the passage's first sentence explains it so clearly.

B.why: He says intelligibility reflects exposure as well as similarity, so similarity still counts. You pushed 'not only similarity' to 'nothing about similarity.'

C.why: His fieldwork found the opposite: one group understood the other far better than it was understood in return.

stem: Based on the text, Varga would most likely agree with which statement about eighteenth-century keyboard sonatas?
stimulus: Histories of eighteenth-century keyboard music usually divide it into two camps: "learned" works built on strict counterpoint for expert listeners, and "galant" works of simple melody for amateur players. Musicologist Ilse Varga argues that this division owes more to nineteenth-century publishers' catalogs than to the composers themselves. In the manuscripts she examined, a single sonata often moved between strict imitation and light, songlike passages, and title pages addressed amateurs and connoisseurs alike.
choices: Learned sonatas were mostly written for experts, while galant sonatas were meant for amateurs.
Composers did not separate the learned and galant styles as sharply as later catalogs did.
The sonatas share so much that no stylistic features can be used to describe them.
Title pages are the most dependable evidence of how a sonata was actually performed.
explanation: Start with Varga's own claim and set aside the view she argues against. She says the learned/galant split comes from later catalogs, not from the composers, because one sonata could mix both styles and one title page could address both audiences. Applied to the sonatas, that means the composers kept the two styles less separate than the catalogs suggest, which is what B says.

A.why: This is the conventional division the passage explains first. Varga is arguing against it, so you picked the view she rejects because the text set it out so clearly.

C.why: Varga says the two styles mix inside a single piece, and she still names them as distinct styles. You pushed 'less separate than claimed' all the way to 'cannot be described at all'.

D.why: Title pages are one supporting detail, and they show who the music was addressed to, not how it was performed. You grabbed an incidental detail and attached a claim the text never makes.

stem: Based on the text, Ríos would most likely agree with which statement about a version of a folktale recorded last year?
stimulus: Folklorists of the historic-geographic school compared hundreds of variants of a tale in an effort to reconstruct its earliest form, treating later versions as drifts away from that original. Folklorist Tomás Ríos takes a different view. Each teller, he argues, reshapes a tale to fit the worries and humor of a particular audience, so a recent version is not a corrupted copy but a complete work. Searching only for the oldest form, he suggests, may obscure what tales do for the communities that tell them.
choices: Its main value lies in what it can reveal about the tale's earliest form.
It proves that the tale never had a single original version anywhere.
It is probably a less faithful record than versions written down a century ago.
It deserves study as a finished work shaped by the community that tells it.
explanation: Ríos's claim is that each teller reshapes a tale for an audience, so a recent version is 'a complete work' and not a corrupted copy. Apply that to a version recorded last year: it is worth studying in its own right, as something shaped by the people who tell it. D extends his argument to the new case.

A.why: Valuing a version for what it shows about the earliest form is the historic-geographic approach that Ríos argues against. You chose the rejected view because the passage explains it first and in detail.

B.why: Ríos says that searching only for the oldest form 'may obscure' something. He never says the tale had no origin, and 'proves' goes well beyond his hedged position.

C.why: Treating later versions as drifts from an original is the very assumption Ríos rejects. In his view a recent version is not a worse copy of an older one.

stem: Based on the text, Lindqvist would most likely agree with which statement about a plant species recently introduced to a region?
stimulus: Conservation policy has often sorted species by origin: those present before human transport are "native" and worth protecting, while recent arrivals are "alien" and targets for removal. Ecologist Amara Lindqvist argues that origin is a poor guide to management. In her long-term surveys of river floodplains, several introduced plants occupied the same niches and supported the same insects as natives, while a few native shrubs spread aggressively after flood control. What matters, she contends, is what a species does where it now grows.
choices: Decisions about managing it should rest on its ecological effects rather than its origin.
It should be removed chiefly because it reached the region only with human help.
It will probably support fewer insects than the native plants growing beside it.
It can be left alone, since introduced plants rarely change the habitats they enter.
explanation: The last sentence states Lindqvist's position: what matters is 'what a species does where it now grows.' Applied to a newly introduced plant, that means you judge it by its ecological effects and not by where it came from. A follows directly from her reasoning.

B.why: Removing a plant because it is an 'alien' arrival is the origin-based policy described in the first sentence, which Lindqvist rejects. You picked the view she argues against.

C.why: Her surveys found that several introduced plants 'supported the same insects as natives.' This choice predicts the opposite of her evidence.

D.why: Lindqvist says to judge a species by its effects. She does not say introduced plants are harmless. You stretched 'origin is a poor guide' into a blanket claim that they rarely matter.

stem: Based on the text, Hamada would most likely agree with which statement about a population of thrushes?
stimulus: Field guides typically label each bird species either a migrant, which leaves its breeding range in winter, or a resident, which stays. Ornithologist Keiko Hamada argues that these labels describe choices rather than kinds of birds. Tracking banded thrushes in a coastal valley over six winters, she found that many individuals departed in cold years and remained in mild ones, and that siblings from the same nest often made different choices.
choices: Each of its members can be permanently classed as either a migrant or a resident.
Its members decide whether to migrate at random, with no link to conditions.
An individual member might leave in one winter and stay through the next.
Field guides should stop describing any of its movements as a form of migration.
explanation: Hamada's claim is that 'migrant' and 'resident' describe choices, not fixed kinds of birds. Her evidence is that the same individuals left in cold years and stayed in mild ones. Applied to any thrush population, that means a single bird could migrate one winter and stay the next, which is what C says.

A.why: Sorting each bird permanently into one category is the field-guide view that Hamada argues against. You chose the conventional labels because the first sentence defines them so clearly.

B.why: Hamada found that birds left in cold years and stayed in mild ones. That is a link to conditions, so 'at random' reverses her finding.

D.why: Hamada says the labels describe choices. She does not say migration doesn't happen or shouldn't be named. You pushed her argument past what she claims.

stem: Based on the text, Castellanos would most likely agree with which statement about efforts to locate the earliest flowering plants?
stimulus: Paleobotanists hunting for the first flowering plants have traditionally searched rock layers for fossil flowers, since petals and stamens make a specimen unmistakable. Paleobotanist Rhea Castellanos considers that approach too narrow. Flowers are fragile and rarely fossilize, she notes, and the earliest flowering plants likely bore small, inconspicuous ones. Distinctive pollen grains and leaf vein patterns, which preserve far more readily, may therefore record the group millions of years before any recognizable flower does.
choices: The best place to find the earliest examples is among well-preserved fossil flowers.
Searches limited to recognizable fossil flowers are likely to miss the earliest examples.
Fossil flowers offer no useful evidence about when flowering plants first appeared.
Flowering plants probably arose later than the oldest known fossil flowers suggest.
explanation: Castellanos calls the flower-only search 'too narrow.' Her reasons are that flowers rarely fossilize, the earliest ones were probably inconspicuous, and pollen and leaf veins may record the group much earlier. It follows that a search confined to recognizable flowers would probably overlook the first flowering plants, which is what B says.

A.why: Searching for fossil flowers is the traditional method that Castellanos criticizes. You picked the approach she rejects because the passage explains why it seemed appealing.

C.why: She calls the flower search too narrow, not useless. You pushed 'not enough on its own' into 'no useful evidence at all'.

D.why: Castellanos suggests that pollen and leaves may record the group millions of years before any flower does. That points to an earlier origin, so this choice reverses her reasoning.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus: Textile historians have long held that the first power looms in 1820s Lancashire multiplied a weaver's output many times over and left hand-loom workers hopelessly behind. Historian Maren Okafor contends that this gap has been overstated. Mill ledgers show that early power looms broke threads so often that an operator, forced to stop and repair them, produced only about twice the cloth of a skilled hand weaver. In Okafor's view, hand weaving faded over decades rather than overnight because the machines' early advantage was modest.
choices: Early power looms let one operator produce many times the cloth of a hand weaver, quickly ending hand weaving.
Okafor argues that early power looms gave operators a far smaller output advantage over hand weavers than historians assume.
Okafor argues that early power looms produced no more cloth than skilled hand weavers did in the same amount of time.
Early power looms broke threads frequently, so operators had to stop the machines and repair them by hand.
explanation: The passage sets up the usual view (a huge output gap), then pivots to Okafor, who says the gap "has been overstated": about twice the cloth, not many times. Everything after the pivot supports her claim about the size of the gap, and choice B states it.

A.why: This is the view Okafor argues against. The passage explains it clearly so that she can reject it, and you took the setup for the author's point.

C.why: You pushed Okafor's claim too far. She says the advantage was about twice the output, which is smaller than assumed but still an advantage. She never says there was no gap.

D.why: This is true, but it's only the evidence for Okafor's argument. It describes one sentence and leaves out her claim about the size of the output gap.

The altitude group's red blood cell counts rose, but its 5,000-meter times improved only about one percent more than the sea-level group's. Runners in Halvorsen's altitude group showed higher red blood cell counts after six weeks of training.
Altitude training gives endurance runners a large performance edge over runners who train at sea level.
Halvorsen's study suggests that altitude training's edge over sea-level training is far smaller than coaches assume.

B.why: This is true, but it's one detail from the study. The passage brings it up only to set up the point that higher blood counts produced little gain in race times.

stem: Based on the text, Valdivia would most likely agree with all of the following EXCEPT:
stimulus: Engineers have long traced metal fatigue to the surface: a scratch concentrates stress, a crack begins there, and polishing is the routine remedy. Materials scientist Ines Valdivia argues that this account fits poorly with 3D-printed aluminum parts. In her tests, most fatigue cracks in printed brackets began at tiny gas pores sealed inside the metal during printing, well beneath the surface. Polishing those brackets, she found, extended their service life only slightly.
choices: Reducing pores formed during printing would likely lengthen a printed bracket's life more than polishing it would.
Surface scratches can still concentrate some stress in a printed aluminum bracket, even if they are not the main problem.
Polishing is the most effective way to delay fatigue cracking in a printed aluminum bracket.
Inspecting only the surface of a printed bracket may miss the flaws most likely to make it fail.
explanation: Valdivia's claim is that in printed aluminum, most cracks start at internal pores, so polishing helps 'only slightly.' Calling polishing the most effective remedy is the conventional surface account she argues against. She would reject it, so it is the exception.

A.why: The text never mentions reducing pores, so this may have looked like it claimed too much. But if pores cause most cracks and polishing barely helps, you can infer that fewer pores would help more. That is her argument applied to a new case, which is exactly what this question asks you to do.

B.why: This mentions surface scratches, so you may have taken it for the view Valdivia rejects. Read it to the end. It only says scratches matter a little, and her finding that polishing helped 'slightly' supports that. She narrows the surface account. She doesn't throw it out.

D.why: Inspection isn't mentioned in the text, so this may have looked unsupported. But the cracks begin 'well beneath the surface,' so checking only the surface would miss them. It follows directly from her finding.

A warehouse with high turnover might gain more from posting shifts early than from a modest raise.
Firms that rely on raises alone to reduce turnover may be using the wrong tool.
How far ahead shifts are posted can affect whether hourly workers stay.

stem: Based on the text, Lindqvist would most likely agree with all of the following EXCEPT:
stimulus: Paleobotanists have traditionally sorted Carboniferous fern-like fossils into two groups: true ferns, which spread by spores, and seed ferns, which bore seeds. Leaf shape was long treated as a reliable guide to which group a fossil belonged to. Paleobotanist Hana Lindqvist challenges that reliance. Examining 300 specimens with preserved reproductive structures, she found nearly identical fronds in both groups, suggesting that leaf shape alone cannot reveal how a plant reproduced.
choices: Fronds of very similar shape could belong to plants that reproduced in different ways.
Spore-bearing and seed-bearing plants of the period really did differ in how they reproduced.
Some fossils assigned to a group on the basis of leaves alone may need to be reexamined.
The difference between true ferns and seed ferns is too slight to be worth recording.
explanation: Lindqvist questions one sorting method, using leaf shape. She does not question the two groups themselves, which she identified by their reproductive structures. Saying the difference isn't worth recording pushes her claim much further than she takes it, so she would reject it.

A.why: This may have looked like a restatement of her evidence rather than her belief. But it is her finding, and she would plainly agree with it. Finding a true statement isn't enough in a NOT question. You need the one that fails.

B.why: This sounds like the traditional view, so you may have assumed she rejects it. She doesn't. She relies on the spore and seed difference to sort her own specimens. What she rejects is leaf shape as a guide to that difference.

C.why: The text doesn't mention reexamining older fossils, so this may have looked like overreach. But if leaf shape can't reveal how a plant reproduced, then assignments based only on leaves are open to doubt. That follows from her claim.
